And being at home is not safe in Kharkiv from the start of the full-scale war waged by Russia, because the Russians can, and do, target apartment buildings and schools with their missiles and artillery. Then, in the city of Kharkiv, the local authorities decided to create classrooms inside the metro stations — so that kids could get education in a safe place. The Kharkiv metro is a deep metro, and it can provide a very good shelter from air raids. The new reality. The first two classrooms in Kharkiv's metro were opened on September 1. On the first day, more than 600 students attended lessons in the subway classrooms. Every morning, at 08.00, about 1,000 of the Kharkiv children were going to the subway classrooms. They are not used to being in shelters — they are too young. "We have created all the conditions here so that children can get education in a very good way. There are all the conditions for comfortable training," notes the Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov. All classrooms are equipped with new computers, so children can connect remotely with teachers and classmates who are abroad. The walls of the metro classrooms are covered with bright pictures with favorite cartoon characters. The classrooms have been renovated with good sound insulation and ventilation. This is a small victory for the city of Kharkiv. But such a small victory matters a lot. It is important for the children and for teachers. Because it’s much more difficult to learn online without communicating with peers, teachers, and seeing a classroom. Education goes on, despite the war. And, what is important, the children can meet their friends. The second Kharkiv school located deep within the city's subway system, and designed to hold up to 900 students, opened last week. The Kharkiv metro is actually the most important part of the city life now. "I’m happy that my daughter goes to school, but I really worry about her,” says parent Yulia. "It is very difficult to sit at home all the time, the child gets bored, and in the classroom we have new things to do, it is interesting and everything is good.” The Kharkiv authorities also announced that they plan to open more subway classes in the near future. The war continues, but the Ukrainians do not give up. The Kharkiv residents have no other choice than to adapt.

How did Putin handle the Kursk submarine disaster? The Kursk submarine disaster, a tragedy that claimed the lives of all 118 crew members, stands as a stark illustration of Vladimir Putin's leadership style – a style that often prioritizes control and image over transparency and genuine human connection with his own people. The event unfolded in August 2000, just months into Putin's presidency, and presented an immediate test of his capacity to lead during a national crisis. The lack of timely information and the subsequent mishandling of the rescue operation, both domestically and internationally, painted a damning portrait of his government. Initially, the Kremlin downplayed the severity of the situation, delaying the acknowledgment of the catastrophe and the offer of international assistance. This hesitancy, this agonizing delay, fueled speculation and distrust, both inside and outside Russia. Families of the sailors waited agonizing days before the official confirmation of the sinking, and then, even longer for any realistic details on the fate of their loved ones. The Russian Navy’s slow, cumbersome response, the technological inadequacies that hampered rescue efforts, and the ultimately futile attempts to save the stranded seamen, were all broadcast on television, and captured the world's attention. The refusal to accept aid from the British and American navies, until several days after the disaster, further obscured the tragic situation. This unwillingness to accept outside help played a significant role in the mounting criticism from the public, who saw it as a display of national pride rather than genuine concern for the lives of those trapped at the bottom of the Barents Sea. Putin’s decision to continue his vacation at a Black Sea resort while the desperate rescue efforts were underway, raised further questions about his priorities and his leadership capabilities. His eventual televised appearance at a meeting with the grieving families, after several days had passed, hardly seemed to soothe their anguish and anger. Instead, it felt like a carefully staged public relations exercise aimed at damage control. Ultimately, Putin's handling of the Kursk disaster revealed a tendency towards secrecy, a penchant for tightly controlling information, and a profound aversion to admitting weakness or failure. It was a critical turning point, exposing his governance style to the Russian people and the world.

Why are so many Russian gullible? What’s wrong with Russians' ability to understand what is going on, and their willingness to support Putin regardless? I remember speaking to a Russian friend immediately after the invasion of Ukraine. “Russians don’t believe in propaganda,” she assured me. One month later, after seeing all the atrocities and war crimes committed by Russian troops in Ukraine, as well as the economic devastation caused by the war, I asked my friend: “Do you still support Putin?” Her reply was: “Yes, of course. It is their war. The West lies, the government tells the truth.” That’s why any Russian, who tells me “the West lies”, immediately loses my trust. And most of all, because I know what I know — and if I know it, it has to be true, right? I recently read on X-Twitter a thread by a Russian journalist, who explained the key reasons why so many Russians are gullible. Here’s what he wrote: «I think that one of the main reasons is the fact that the vast majority of Russians have a very low level of trust in other people (and in principle they have no trust in institutions). Trust is the basis of any cooperation. Because of the lack of trust, the society is atomized. This attitude is not the result of Putin’s propaganda. Russians have had little trust in each other since Soviet times, at least. And this mindset can be easily manipulated through the manipulation of fear. The state, being distrusted, becomes the only hope for a person in the conditions of high unpredictability. The state promises order, but often, it’s a false promise, leading to more chaos. The less interpersonal trust, the more loyalty to authorities. In the West, the law is above everything else. If you break the law, you are punished, and public reaction is very important. In Russia, the law is not designed to protect people, and it's applied selectively. The authorities don't need to be trusted, they just need to be feared. People trust the one who is capable of ensuring their protection. And the strongest is always right. So when state (or Putin in this case), promises protection, people believe more, even after seeing the opposite.» (End quote.) This thread makes sense to me. Russians don’t trust other people, or institutions. They only trust the strongest, the one who guarantees to save them — or at least, to pretend that he guarantees to save them. Putin. This is what makes so many Russians gullible. This is what makes so many Russians support Putin.

How likely is it that Ukraine has secretly prepared dirty bombs with nuclear material as a last line of defence against the Russian nuclear attack? I am unable to formulate an answer to the question, because I don’t believe that Ukraine secretly prepared dirty bombs with nuclear materials as a last line of defense against the Russian nuclear attack.

Why did Muscovy change its name to Russia? The Grand Duchy of Moscow, or Muscovy, as it was known in the West, was a regional power that steadily expanded its territory, absorbing neighboring principalities. Its rulers, the Tsars, styled themselves as successors to the Byzantine Emperors, inheriting their ambition to become the “Third Rome.” This imperial aspiration played a crucial role in the rebranding. Officially, the name "Russia" was adopted in 1721 by Tsar Peter the Great, following his victory in the Great Northern War. Peter, a fervent admirer of Western European culture and technology, wanted to modernize his realm and integrate it into the European system. He considered the name "Muscovy" outdated, as a term used by foreigners, and the term “Russia” more sophisticated, associating it with a larger political identity and emphasizing a connection to the historical legacy of Kyivan Rus, which predated Muscovy, though the relationship was often contested and selectively emphasized for political reasons. He also wanted to create a unified national identity. This transformation was not merely linguistic; it reflected a profound shift in the country's political orientation and ambitions. It was about presenting itself not just as a regional power, but as an empire with a global presence and a destiny tied to the grandest traditions of European civilization. The Tsars weren't just renaming a territory; they were rebranding a whole civilization, crafting a new image, and rewriting a history to fit their grand design.

Has Quora been targeted by Putin trolls? So many questions lately are just risible idiotic nonsense. Are Quora’s algorithms now catering to pro-Russian propaganda? One can’t help but notice a marked increase in the prominence of absurd queries and utterly nonsensical responses lately. Many posts reek of a manufactured authenticity, designed to sow discord and misinform. The sheer volume and blatant absurdity of it all suggests a concerted effort, a campaign. Whether it’s Kremlin-paid trolls or simply useful idiots, the effect is the same: undermining truth and muddying the waters. The goal, I suspect, is to destabilize, to create doubt, and to erode trust in democratic institutions. These trolls are not interested in reasoned debate or genuine exchange; they are agents of chaos spreading disinformation. They are not interested in answering questions, but in creating them, ones that are designed to inflame divisions and propagate a distorted view of reality. It's infuriating, frankly. This deluge of idiocy is a direct assault on the pursuit of knowledge and truth, and it is the responsibility of Quora to take action. The platform should vigorously and vehemently defend the space for free thought and responsible inquiry.

How would the provision of Patriot air defence systems affect the situation in the city of Kharkiv? The provision of these advanced systems could be a game-changer, potentially offering a shield against the relentless barrage of Russian missiles and drones that have become the city's grim daily reality. Kharkiv, a city of grit and defiance, has been subjected to relentless attacks, and the presence of Patriot systems would undoubtedly bolster its defenses. These systems represent more than just military hardware; they symbolize a commitment to protect civilian lives and critical infrastructure. They could provide a much-needed respite, allowing residents to breathe a collective sigh of relief, and giving them a semblance of normalcy. The psychological impact alone would be enormous, fostering a sense of security and resilience in the face of constant threat. However, the deployment of Patriots wouldn't be a magic bullet, as the war isn't just about air defense. The city still contends with ground attacks and other forms of aggression. Yet, they would represent a powerful tool in the hand of Ukrainian forces, further solidifying Kharkiv’s position and providing the city an opportunity for a future.

What is wrong with the Russian government? “There is nothing new under the sun.” This is what the Russian government thinks, it seems. Or, more precisely, the people around Vladimir Putin. They repeat the mistakes of the Soviet Union. They are very much inspired, of course, by the Soviet propaganda. The most vivid example of the Soviet propaganda is the story of Pavlik Morozov, who denounced his own parents to the authorities, and was then killed by relatives, and was then turned into a hero and a martyr for the Soviet regime. Today, the children inform on their parents in Russia — because, for all those who didn’t leave the country, the children are the only family members who are not brainwashed by the state propaganda. The Russian government is doing everything it can to isolate Russia from the outside world and make it a giant North Korea — or Soviet Union, again. The government wants its citizens to believe that the West is evil, and they must be protected from it. Russian TV channels broadcast that Russia is at war with the West, not with Ukraine. The Russian government doesn't believe that the truth matters. The Russian government treats its population as cattle. The Russian government doesn’t care about its own soldiers. The Russian government doesn’t care about its wounded soldiers. The Russian government doesn’t care about the mothers and wives of the soldiers who were killed in Ukraine. The Russian government doesn’t care about its own people. The Russian government cares about the money — and the power. If someone disagrees with the government, they shut them up — permanently. If someone is saying bad things about the war, they are put in prison. If someone says bad things about President Putin, they are put in prison, or killed. The Russian government wants to be feared, not loved. The Russian government wants to be obeyed, not discussed. The Russian government is a dictatorship. The Russian government wants to be in charge, always. The Russian government is a corrupt and criminal organization that happens to have a country. This is what is wrong with the Russian government.

What the hell is going on in Russia? Is it the case that Medvedev drinks a lot? We must do everything we can so that Ukraine's "irreversible path" to NATO ends with either Ukraine or NATO disappearing. Preferably both, he writes on social media. And then the former Russian president, Dmitry Medvedev, adds a cherry on top: "After all, it’s all the fault of the weak, submissive, and spineless West". Medvedev is indeed on a roll. "The goals of the special military operation will be achieved in the name of peace, stability, and the flourishing of the Ukrainian people," he proclaims. Is that a joke? The guy believes his own lies. Or perhaps he doesn't, and is just trolling us all. But anyway... On December 27, Medvedev added that the "denazification" of Ukraine is "one of Russia's basic and undeniable goals." And that the main goal is to make sure that “Ukraine will no longer be our enemy, that it will never again threaten Russia”. So… the destruction of Ukrainians, their language, culture, history, and very existence? Is that what he means? Hard to tell, but at least the meaning is clear. Medvedev is not the only one. The state-run media and even many private media outlets in Russia have been filled with increasingly bellicose rhetoric since the beginning of the war in Ukraine. The voices of reason are being silenced; the voices of hate are growing louder and louder. The propaganda is so blatant and so pervasive that it’s difficult to imagine how anyone could believe the official narrative. But millions of Russians do, and they are being whipped into a frenzy of nationalistic fervor. What will happen next? No one knows. But one thing is certain: Russia is on a dangerous path, and the world needs to be prepared for the worst. The longer the war in Ukraine continues, the more likely it is that the situation will get worse, not better. Meanwhile, in Russia...

What would happen to Russia if Putin were to die tomorrow? The question itself is fraught, isn't it? To ponder the demise of a leader, to speculate on the ripple effects of such a seismic event, feels almost… improper. But given the current global chessboard, the whispers of potential successors, and the sheer unpredictability of the Russian bear, it's a question that lingers, doesn't it? One thing seems certain: Russia would become a wild card, a country where anything could happen. The power vacuum alone would be a tempest, a free-for-all. The vultures, both domestic and international, would be circling, eager to feast on the carcass of a weakened state. And by carcasses, I mean territories, resources, influence, everything. The various oligarchs — already accustomed to wielding power behind the scenes — would be the first to jostle for position, each with their own agenda and their own private armies. Those forces that were already fighting in Ukraine would stop fighting because the reason of that war, Vladimir Putin, would be gone. The war in Ukraine would end, and the sanctions against Russia would be gone. The Western countries would rejoice. But whether or not they would be happy for long – that remains to be seen. I don't believe Russia would immediately collapse, not in a complete implosion. No, the more likely scenario — at least initially — is a period of intense instability, a dark age, I’d say. There might be even a civil war. Maybe not a full-blown, all-out conflagration, but rather a series of localized conflicts, power struggles, and purges. Think of it this way: imagine a pressure cooker exploding, sending shards of shrapnel in every direction. Some of those fragments might cut deep, drawing blood. Some may cause destruction. If Russia somehow avoided all this, or if it did, at it ended quickly, then…well, then you still have to deal with Russia. Because Putin's death might not trigger genuine reform. It might simply usher in a new, equally ruthless leader, someone who’s just as keen to maintain the status quo or even consolidate power further through an even tougher hand. And then, you’d still face the same challenges — the same internal contradictions, the same imperial ambitions, the same simmering resentment. The world would breathe a sigh of relief. But that sigh might turn into a gasp very quickly.

Do you think Viktor Orbán's proposal for a ceasefire in Ukraine is genuine? Viktor Orbán, the Hungarian Prime Minister, has a knack for making waves, doesn't he? His recent pronouncements regarding a ceasefire in Ukraine have certainly caused a stir. Is it genuine? That's the million-dollar question, isn't it? On the surface, a call for peace seems like a noble gesture, a beacon of hope amidst the ongoing devastation. One might be tempted to applaud, to see it as a desperate plea to halt the bloodshed. But with Orbán, nothing is ever quite that straightforward. His history of cozying up to Putin, of obstructing EU sanctions, of generally playing the role of the Kremlin's useful idiot, casts a long, dark shadow over any such declaration. Is this a genuine attempt to find a resolution, or simply another calculated move designed to sow discord, to undermine Western unity, and to further his own agenda? Frankly, based on his past actions and geopolitical maneuvers, I'm more inclined to suspect the latter. This could very well be a smokescreen, a tactic designed to muddy the waters, to buy Putin time, or to weaken support for Ukraine. Orbán thrives on controversy, on positioning himself as the contrarian. Let's not forget his consistent efforts to destabilize Europe's cohesion. I would consider his ceasefire proposal with a hefty dose of skepticism.

During the Red Terror and Stalin's later purges, what made one end up on the kill lists? How could one protect oneself from ending up dead or in the Gulag? It was simple, yet terrifyingly complex. The criteria for inclusion on those lists, the very basis of life or death, were as arbitrary as they were absolute. A neighbor's jealous whisper, a perceived disloyalty, a joke told in the wrong company – any infraction, real or imagined, could seal your fate. Family members, friends, and even casual acquaintances were potential threats, their words – your potential demise. Denunciation was the most common weapon, fueled by fear and self-preservation. To survive, one had to be a chameleon, to blend seamlessly into the background, avoid any hint of individuality, any spark of independent thought. Every interaction was to be carefully calibrated, every word measured, scrutinizing, and sanitized. Knowledge of those in power was paramount, their moods, their whims, their hidden agendas were all vital factors. One needed to cultivate a network of dubious alliances, to know who to bribe, who to feign loyalty to, who to avoid altogether. Keeping your head down, your mouth shut, and your eyes open was the rule. But even the most meticulous precautions offered no guarantees. There were always the unpredictable turns of the tide -- a change in political winds that could sweep away the most careful plans. In the end, survival hinged on the cruelest of lotteries: sheer, dumb luck.

How can Russians be neo-Nazis when Russia suffered at the hands of Nazis in WWII? It’s a question that echoes with a bitter irony, a cruel twist of historical fate. To witness the very nation that bore the brunt of Nazi aggression now accused of mirroring those dark ideologies—it's a cognitive dissonance that's hard to reconcile. The sheer scale of the suffering inflicted upon the Soviet Union during the Second World War, the staggering loss of life, the scorched earth, the systematic cruelty – these are scars that run so deep, they should serve as a constant, visceral reminder of the evils of fascism, of the absolute necessity of fighting against it. Yet, here we are, confronted with accusations of a resurgent neo-Nazism emerging from the heart of Russia. It’s a confounding paradox. How do you square the historical narrative of heroic resistance with the contemporary actions of a government that seems to selectively embrace and employ some of the rhetoric and tactics of its former tormentors? How can a nation that saw twenty-seven million of its citizens perish fight a war of aggression against a democratic neighbor? How can the memory of the Siege of Leningrad be invoked while cities in Ukraine are reduced to rubble? This is a question that’s riddled with complexities, with hypocrisy, and with a chilling disregard for the lessons of the past.

Was socialism a failed experiment? It's a question that sparks heated debate, with arguments on both sides often veering into the abstract. Those who champion socialism tout its ideals of equality and social welfare, pointing to the successes of the Nordic model, with its robust social safety nets. Yet, even these lauded examples wrestle with the practical challenges of high taxation and the potential for diminished economic incentives. On the other hand, critics of socialism frequently cite the historical failures of centrally planned economies, where inefficiency and shortages were commonplace. The collapse of the Soviet Union stands as a stark reminder of the economic pitfalls of such systems. But here's the crux: are these historical examples truly indicative of the core principles of socialism, or were they deviations, corrupted by authoritarianism and a lack of democratic checks? It's tempting to fall into the trap of historical determinism, to judge an entire ideology based on the actions of a few, or on the particular circumstances of a bygone era. And isn't it more complicated than a simple 'yes' or 'no'? Economic systems, like societies, evolve. Perhaps socialism, in its various manifestations, can be seen as a work-in-progress, constantly adapting and re-evaluating its approaches. Or perhaps the inherent flaws of central planning inevitably outweigh the perceived benefits. Ultimately, the answer to this question depends on your definition of socialism, your willingness to consider nuance, and, perhaps most importantly, your interpretation of history.

If Russia succeeded in dissolving Ukraine would there be insurgency with enough support like the Taliban? Would Russian troops be trapped in cities? How long would it take Russia to turn Ukraine into a fully submissive Russian territory? I'm not sure what the exact answers to these questions are, but I can tell you this. Even if Russia were "successful" in conquering Ukraine, it would be a poisoned victory. Ukraine has a strong national identity, forged through centuries of struggle and a deep desire for self-determination. Erasing that, even through brutal force, is a fantasy. The Ukrainians have proven their willingness to fight for their freedom; they have demonstrated their ingenuity in the face of overwhelming odds. Any occupation would be met with resistance, both open and covert. Guerrilla warfare, sabotage, and acts of defiance would become a constant headache for Moscow. Russian troops, stretched thin, would find themselves bogged down in a costly and bloody quagmire. Turning Ukraine into a compliant territory would take years, maybe decades, and at what cost? The human cost would be catastrophic, measured in lives lost, families shattered, and a nation's spirit crushed. Russia might control the land, but it would never control the hearts and minds of the Ukrainian people. The seeds of future unrest would be sown, creating an ongoing struggle for dominance that would never truly end. Think about Afghanistan, and the decades of turmoil that followed the Soviet invasion. The parallels are stark. The complexities of the Ukrainian spirit and their deep-rooted desire for freedom cannot be simply dismissed. The cost for the Russian Federation would outweigh any perceived gains. The invasion and a protracted occupation would turn out to be a massive strategic blunder. The longer the invasion goes on, the worse the outcome will ultimately be for Russia.

How badly has Putin damaged Russia? The damage is incalculable. Beyond the immediate horrors of the war in Ukraine, the economic devastation wrought by sanctions, and the international isolation that has become Russia's new reality, there's a deeper, more insidious corrosion at work. It's a moral and intellectual decay that threatens to unravel the very fabric of Russian society. The suppression of dissent, the relentless propaganda, the rewriting of history, and the demonization of the West – these are the tools Putin has employed to tighten his grip on power. But they have also poisoned the well of truth and reason, leaving behind a society increasingly detached from reality. Ask any Russian, "How are you?". The answer will be, "Fine." They won't tell you about friends and family members lost to the war, neighbors disappeared by state security, or the constant barrage of propaganda. They won't reveal their fears or doubts, for to do so would be to invite suspicion and, potentially, punishment. And if they do not answer "Fine," they will be thrown in prison just for that. The cost of silence is high, but the price of speaking out is often higher. This is not just a political crisis; it's a crisis of the soul. A nation that once prided itself on its literature, its art, and its intellectual prowess is now reduced to a caricature of its former self. The vibrant civic life that once flickered to life, however briefly, has been snuffed out. The independent media, once the lifeblood of a free society, is now a state mouthpiece. Putin isn't just destroying Ukraine; he's destroying Russia from within. His legacy will not be one of strength or glory, but of shame and self-inflicted wounds. The Russia that emerges from this dark chapter will be a husk of its former self, a fractured, fearful nation struggling to come to terms with the damage wrought by one man’s ambition. The war in Ukraine has provided the world with irrefutable proof of the "Russian world," a world of cruelty, lies, and brutality. It has also shown that the Kremlin’s ability to manipulate, to corrupt, and to inflict pain is virtually limitless, and that it is driven by a deep-seated rage. And while Russia's eventual fate remains uncertain, one thing is clear: Putin has irrevocably damaged his country's future.

How does Russia use social media as a strategy? Russian propaganda has always been a relentless, multi-pronged beast, and social media is simply the newest battlefield in its ongoing campaign to sow chaos and confusion. It's less about delivering a coherent, easily digestible message, and more about sheer volume, flooding the internet with conflicting narratives and fabricated "facts" until a miasma of doubt obscures the truth. Think of it not as a carefully aimed sniper shot, but as a shotgun blast, hoping to hit something—anything—that will destabilize the targeted societies. The goal? To erode trust in institutions, weaponize existing social divisions, and ultimately, undermine any sense of shared reality. Russian operatives are masters of anonymity, creating a Byzantine web of fake accounts, bots, and troll farms. They skillfully exploit existing online echo chambers, amplifying divisive talking points and pushing them into the mainstream. They masterfully play on emotions, leveraging fear, anger, and resentment to amplify the reach of their disinformation. These manipulations aren't always crude. They tailor the narratives and the accounts to suit the specific audience. For example, they are more aggressive in certain regions in targeting specific vulnerabilities to create chaos. They often employ an arsenal of memes and short videos designed to spread like wildfire—information or mis-information, it doesn't matter as long as it creates impact. A key part of their approach is to flood the zone with noise, to drown out any dissenting voices or evidence that could undermine the narrative. The truth becomes just another opinion, another possible perspective in the swirling vortex of manufactured "news." Russian social media strategy is the embodiment of cynicism: a calculated assault on truth itself. It's a war of attrition fought with pixels and algorithms, and unless we recognize it for what it is, we risk losing the very ground beneath our feet.

Will the USA continue to support Ukraine after Trump takes office? It’s a question that hangs heavy in the air, a chilling uncertainty that threatens the very fabric of Ukraine’s fight for survival. The specter of a Trump presidency looms, casting a long shadow over the unwavering support Ukraine has received from the United States. We're left to wonder if the current trajectory, the vital flow of aid and weaponry, will be abruptly halted, altered, or diminished. The potential implications are dire. The Ukrainian military, currently locked in a brutal war against a far larger foe, relies on this support. American assistance is not just a financial lifeline, but a critical infusion of advanced military technology, intelligence, and training. Should that assistance wane, the consequences could be devastating, potentially extending the conflict, emboldening Russia, and costing countless more lives. The narrative of this war could shift dramatically, potentially reshaping the geopolitical landscape. What about the bipartisan consensus that has largely driven American policy? Will it fracture under the weight of a new administration? Or will the inherent principles of democratic governance and the strategic importance of Ukraine’s defense ultimately prevail? The uncertainty is excruciating, a constant weight on the shoulders of those fighting for freedom. The future of Ukraine, perhaps, hinges on the decisions made by a single man. These are uneasy days, filled with both trepidation and a desperate hope that the ties that bind the two nations will endure.

What is the United Nations doing about Russia? The UN, in its lumbering, often frustrating dance of diplomacy, has become a stage for the unfolding tragedy that is Russia's war in Ukraine. While the world body, designed to prevent such conflicts, often feels powerless, it remains the crucial space where the international community attempts to address matters related to this war. The speeches delivered, the resolutions passed (or vetoed), and the behind-the-scenes deals struck by diplomats are a constant, if sometimes ineffective, flurry of activity. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has been involved, with Ukraine bringing charges of genocide against Russia. The International Criminal Court (ICC) has warrants out for the arrest of Vladimir Putin and his children. Human rights organizations have been meticulously documenting atrocities, adding their voices to the chorus of condemnation directed at Moscow. Much of the UN’s action is focused on humanitarian aid, providing assistance to the millions of Ukrainians displaced both inside and outside the country – despite the challenges of delivering aid in an active war zone, especially to those in areas under Russian control. Sanctions, too, are a major tool. The UN Security Council, hampered by Russia's veto power, has had significant limitations in fully implementing sanctions to the extent some members would like; however, the global impact of sanctions imposed by individual nations working within the framework of the UN still has the power to cripple the Russian war machine. The problem, of course, is that any attempt to hold Russia accountable faces the stubborn reality of Russia’s permanent seat on the Security Council, a position that grants them the power to block resolutions. This inherent contradiction between the UN’s mandate and its structure is on vivid display. The UN’s role is to be judged on what they have prevented; but they are judged on what they fail to prevent. The very fact that the UN exists, even if it is ineffective, is important. In the end, the UN's efforts, though often appearing inadequate in the face of such large events, are a necessary and essential platform for seeking justice, providing aid, and attempting to maintain some semblance of international order amidst the chaos.

Why is Viktor Yanukovych (former President of Ukraine) meeting with Lukashenko in Belarus today (24 May 2024)? Well, Yanukovych’s meeting with Lukashenko, as reported by Belarusian media, is just another bewildering episode in the ongoing saga of post-revolution Ukraine. It’s a master class in the art of political theater, a performance that only fuels further cynicism from those who continue to observe and hope for change. Some might suggest that this meeting, which coincided with a planned visit by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Portugal, is a sign of thawing relations, or perhaps a secret negotiation, a carefully orchestrated behind-the-scenes drama of power play, but I don’t buy it. It felt more likely that Yanukovych, a man ousted from power after the 2014 Euromaidan Revolution, a man with blood on his hands, and subsequently indicted on charges of treason, is trying to remain relevant, hoping to insert himself back into the political game a decade later, and using his dubious connections to puppet Putin’s ally Lukashenko as a gateway. It’s possible that this "meeting" is nothing more than a choreographed attempt to muddy the waters and undermine Ukraine’s standing on the world stage, but I would suspect this stunt has the blessing of his Kremlin masters. Yanukovych, like Putin, has no moral compass; perhaps, the meeting is just a calculated move designed to stir up old wounds and remind us all of a past many Ukrainians would rather forget. The timing is almost too perfect, isn't it? A day when all eyes should be on Ukraine’s future, this unwelcome distraction appears. His presence serves mostly as a chilling reminder of how close Ukraine came to losing it all. And now, Ukraine needs to shake it off and keep moving forward.

Did NATO promise Russia not to expand eastwards? The question of NATO's eastward expansion is a complex one, steeped in historical interpretation and conflicting narratives. The official stance of NATO has consistently been that no formal, legally binding promises were ever made to Russia. Yet, the Kremlin vehemently disagrees, pointing to assurances given by Western leaders in the late 1980s and early 1990s as the Soviet Union was collapsing and the Warsaw Pact was dissolving. Those assurances, according to Russia – and many historians – were that NATO would not expand "one inch eastward." The exact wording, the context, and the parties involved in these alleged agreements are all subjects of contention, making it an almost impossible task to find common ground for both sides. This disagreement is not just about semantics. It lies at the heart of the current crisis and fuels the mistrust between Russia and the West. The United States and NATO member states argue that NATO's expansion is a matter for sovereign nations to decide, and that Russia has no right to dictate the security arrangements of its neighbors. But Russia sees NATO's expansion as a direct threat, a violation of its perceived sphere of influence, and a broken promise that has brought the alliance right up to its borders. The narrative, as told by Russia, paints a picture of a West that is deliberately encircling and weakening Russia. The expansion eastward has been a gradual process, with numerous countries joining the alliance since the end of the Cold War. Each expansion has been met with protests and warnings from Russia, growing steadily more strident as the alliance moved closer and closer to its borders. This ongoing conflict is rooted in different interpretations of history, security and international law. Who is right and who is wrong? The truth, as always, is a tangled web of competing interests and ambiguous promises.

Does Putin really rely on body doubles? In the realm of potentates and potentates-in-waiting, the concept of a body double isn't merely a fantastical notion conjured by Hollywood scripts; it often dances on the periphery of stark reality. Vladimir Putin, a figure steeped in mystique and guarded by layers of secrecy, has, for a considerable time, been the subject of such speculation. Whispers of "Putin doubles" have swelled within both the public and private spheres, fueled by purported inconsistencies in his appearance, gait, and overall demeanor during public appearances. These suppositions amplify the intrigue surrounding the Russian leader, painting a picture of a man who may be shielding not only his physical self, but also his health, motives, and even his authority, beneath a carefully crafted facade. The crux of the matter isn't solely about whether a proxy exists, but why. Is it driven by health concerns, the desire to evade security threats, or an attempt to shape a desired narrative? These lingering queries have captivated both political analysts and the general populace, spawning myriad theories that only serve to deepen the enigmatic aura surrounding the Kremlin. Whether these doubles are genuine is almost immaterial. The very fact that such rumors persist is a potent illustration of the closed nature of Putin’s Russia, and the pervasive uncertainty that surrounds it.
